description: Our team is tackling the challenge of building health monitoring software tailored for astronauts on deep-space missions. We are creating a functional, user-friendly digital system to monitor biometrics, well-being, and physiological trends in microgravity. We are looking for team members interested in software development, biomedical data, UI/UX, or project storytelling.
summary:
ChascaCan is a crew health decision-support interface for missions where
Earth cannot answer in time. On a Mars transit a one-way signal takes 22
minutes, so a crew member who needs a decision has to make it on board.

It separates two things most monitoring systems merge into a single
confidence number: how serious a situation is, and how well the available
evidence supports that judgement. A lost or faulty sensor lowers the
support, never the severity. A module with no instrument reads "no data"
rather than "stable", because stable is a claim that requires a
measurement.

Every threshold on screen states its source and who set it. Where we have
not verified a value, the screen says "pending verification" instead of
showing a plausible number.

The radiation module runs on measured NASA data: 36,364 one-minute dose
readings from the ALTEA-Survey instrument aboard the ISS, obtained through
NASA OSDR, evaluated against the 600 mSv career limit in NASA-STD-3001
Vol 1 [V1 4030]. Crew physiology is simulated and labelled as such.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

ChascaCan is a crew health decision-support interface for missions where

Earth cannot answer in time. It runs two independent axes

SEVERITY answers "how bad is this": STABLE, WATCH, ACTION, IMMEDIATE.

ALERT SUPPORT answers "how sure are we": LIMITED, MODERATE, STRONG.

They never move together. When the HRV chest strap stops reporting, the

cognitive-readiness alert stays at ACTION and the support falls to

MODERATE, with the reason shown on screen. A module with no instrument

reads "no data", never "stable", because stable is a claim that requires

a measurement. Four of the ten modules read "no data · no sensor or rule".

PROVENANCE ON EVERY RULE

Each alert shows where its threshold comes from and who set it: either

"NASA standard" with the requirement number, or "ChascaCan definition".

For the cabin oxygen guardrail the applicable lower bound has not been

verified against the source table, so the field reads "pending

verification" instead of a number. We shipped that gap visibly.

MEASURED NASA DATA

The radiation module is not simulated. It runs on 36,364 one-minute dose

readings from the ALTEA-Survey instrument in the ISS US Laboratory,

obtained through NASA OSDR. Two of the 28 days were excluded by our own

85% completeness requirement, leaving 26 days at 97.1% measured

completeness. The cumulative 23.14 mSv is evaluated against the 600 mSv

career limit in NASA-STD-3001 Volume 1 and shown as 3.9%

of it.

That rule was written before we had real data. The first time it ran

against flight data it rejected two days on its own, and we did not lower

the threshold to keep them.

WHAT WE DO NOT CLAIM

Crew physiology is simulated and every screen says so. ISS dose rates

understate a Mars transit, because the ISS sits inside Earth's

magnetosphere; our radiation figure is a lower bound, not a Mars

estimate. The radiation module uses a single instrument with no

redundancy, so its support is limited and says why.

TOOLS

Figma Make (React, TypeScript, CSS) for the interface. JavaScript for the

decision engine. Python for processing the radiation dataset. Interface

in Spanish, Turkish and English.

WHY IT IS DIFFERENT

Most monitoring tools become more confident as they lose information,

because a missing input quietly drops out of the average. ChascaCan does

the opposite: it becomes more cautious and says so. We deliberately used

no language model anywhere in the decision path, because every number on

screen must be traceable to a source and a generated sentence cannot be.

ABOUT THE TEAM

Built by two students in different countries — one in Ica, Peru and one

in Istanbul, Turkey — working eight time zones apart. We never worked in

the same room. Building a tool for someone who cannot reach the people

who could help them was not an abstract problem for us.
